mainEntity.name: How long should dental bonding typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental bonding generally lasts between 3-7 years, though this varies significantly based on location, oral habits, and maintenance. Front teeth bonding often lasts longer than back teeth due to lower bite forces. Regular dental care and avoiding damaging habits can help maximise longevity.

mainEntity.name: Can chipped bonding be repaired, or does it need complete replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Small chips in bonding can often be repaired by adding new composite material and reshaping the restoration. However, if the bonding has failed extensively or if decay has developed underneath, complete replacement may be necessary. Your dentist will assess the specific situation during examination.

mainEntity.name: Why does bonding on some teeth discolour faster than others?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bonding discolouration occurs more rapidly on teeth exposed to staining substances like coffee, tea, or tobacco. Front teeth, which come into direct contact with beverages and foods, may stain faster than back teeth. The quality of the composite material and finishing also affects stain resistance.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for bonding to feel rough after several years?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some surface roughening of bonding material over time is normal due to wear from chewing and brushing. However, significant roughness or sharp edges should be evaluated by a dentist, as this may indicate deterioration that requires attention to prevent further damage.

mainEntity.name: Can grinding my teeth at night damage bonding even if I don't notice it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, nocturnal bruxism often occurs unconsciously and can generate significant forces that damage bonding. Many people are unaware they grind their teeth during sleep. If you wake with jaw soreness or notice premature bonding wear, discuss nightguard options with your dentist.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between bonding failure and normal wear?

acceptedAnswer.text: Normal wear appears as gradual smoothing and minor surface changes over time. Bonding failure typically involves chipping, cracking, or complete detachment from the tooth surface. Any sudden changes, sharp edges, or sensitivity suggest failure rather than normal wear and require dental evaluation.
